nodes.label: Data Network Effects
nodes.definition: User activity continuously improves the product’s performance, creating a self-reinforcing advantage via accumulated data.

nodes.label: Algorithmic Opacity
nodes.definition: Vendors obscure the inner workings of algorithms to prevent replication, audit, or substitution.

nodes.label: Information Asymmetry
nodes.definition: Vendors selectively reveal or manipulate performance and telemetry metrics to control narratives or regulation.

nodes.label: Ecosystem Envelopment
nodes.definition: Absorbing adjacent services and tools into a unified platform to control complementary layers of the value chain.

nodes.label: Strategic Interoperability
nodes.definition: Allowing partial interoperability—enough to attract users but insufficient for full substitution.

nodes.label: Ecosystem Gravity
nodes.definition: Network effects reinforced by social identity and shared assets, turning participation into dependency.

nodes.label: Standard Capture
nodes.definition: Dominating standards bodies to steer 'open' protocols in ways that favor proprietary implementations.

nodes.label: Continuous Integration Drift
nodes.definition: Frequent, incremental API or service updates that gradually erode third-party compatibility.

nodes.label: Loss-Leader Infrastructure
nodes.definition: Offering below-cost infrastructure or compute to onboard workloads and lock in market share.

nodes.label: Regulatory Arbitrage
nodes.definition: Exploiting gaps between legal jurisdictions or slow-moving regulators to operate ahead of compliance.

edges.relation: Data accumulation increases the feasibility and incentive to hide algorithms.
Opacity directly drives asymmetry by controlling what is observable.
Control of information allows strategic expansion and acquisition without market alarm.
Once vertical integration is achieved, partial interoperability maximizes capture.
Partial openness builds user momentum and cross-platform dependency.
Control over multiple stack layers grants leverage in standards-setting bodies.
Captured standards enable version drift under the guise of compliance.
Compatibility friction pushes users deeper into the vendor ecosystem.
Subsidized infrastructure attracts new workloads that feed envelopment.
Aggressive pricing exploits timing gaps before antitrust or subsidy regulations adapt.
Social and economic dominance legitimizes influence over standards.
Opaque algorithms make it harder for open standards to compete on clarity.
Withholding key data delays regulatory detection or enforcement.
Legal flexibility enables risk-taking in pricing or market expansion.
